list.listitem: The identification and treatment of hypertension is a cornerstone of the prevention and management of cerebrovascular disease (CVD).A
For the diagnosis of CVD, combined MRA and carotid duplex ultrasound is accurate and less invasive than digital subtraction angiography.C
For primary prevention of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), low-dose aspirin is recommended in those with vascular disease or diabetes.A
For secondary prevention of stroke or TIA, antiplatelet therapy is recommended, or anticoagulation for those with atrial fibrillation.A
Consider carotid endarterectomy or stenting for selected symptomatic patients with at least 70% carotid stenosis.A
Blood pressure reduction, regardless of modality, is a cornerstone of management of CVD.A

background.definition: CVD occurs when blood supply to the brain is insufficient due to atherosclerosis, aneurysms, or clots in the vessels supplying the territories of the brain. Patients with CVD are at risk for stroke, a neurologic deficit that results from focal vascular injury. This chapter focuses on chronic management; other chapters address management of acute stroke and TIA.

list.listitem: A total of 610,000 new cases of stroke occur each year in the United States.

The prevalence of silent cerebral infarction between the ages of 55 and 64 years is approximately 11%. This prevalence increases to 22% between the ages of 65 and 69 years, 28% between the ages of 70 and 74 years, 32% between the ages of 75 and 79 years, 40% between the ages of 80 and 84 years, and 43% in those older than 85 years.
Applying these rates to 1998 US population estimates results in an estimated 13 million people with prevalent silent stroke.
There were $34 billion in costs attributable to patients who suffered a stroke.
CVD is the third leading cause of death for men and women in the United States.
The prevalence of caregiver burden in one meta-analysis was 25% to 54% and remained elevated for an indefinite period following stroke.
Uncontrolled hypertension is a major cause of CVD and stroke
Diabetes
Hyperlipidemia
Tobacco use
Atrial fibrillation

In a large population-based observational study, women who used levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs were less likely to have ischemic strokes than nonusers of hormonal contraception. There was no significant association with ICH.
Darbepoeitin therapy for anemia in diabetic subjects with chronic kidney disease is associated with an increased risk of stroke when compared to placebo (NNT for harm = 49 over 29 months).

Studies have found large increases in the likelihood of vascular events in patients hospitalized with COVID-19, including stroke, and especially if they spent time in the ICU. For cerebrovascular disease, the excess burdens per 1000 in the year following infection are 3, 20, and 31 events for nonhospitalized, hospitalized, and ICU patients, respectively.
Most acute stroke is ischemic rather than hemorrhagic (85% vs 15% respectively).
Only 1 in 5 strokes is due to large artery stenosis, particulary in Caucasian and Asian patients. Atherosclerotic plaque is largely to blame in CVD of large intracranial and extracranial vessels.

Small vessel ischemic disease results from lipohyalinosis of intracerebral penetrating arteries. Lipid hyaline buildup occurs downstream in vessels secondary to systemic hypertension. Small vessel disease is a common cause of CVD in African-American patients.
Other less common causes of CVD include amyloid formation, aneurysmal dilatation, and inflammation resulting from cerebral vasculitides.
A common cause of embolic stroke is atrial fibrillation. Less common is paradoxical embolus from a VTE and undiagnosed patent foramen ovale (PFO).

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Recent initiation of a triptan drug for migraine

list.listitem: Modifiable risk factors such as smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and obesity should be addressed.B
Aspirin is recommended as primary prevention for stroke in those at sufficiently high risk (e.g., those with vascular disease or diabetes).A
Treat hypertension and hyperlipidemia according to national guidelines.A
The harms of screening for carotid artery disease outweigh benefits in asymptomatic patients.A

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends against screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis in the general adult population because the harms of the screening and resultant treatment outweigh the benefits of screening.
Screen adolescents and adults at least every 2 years for hypertension, tobacco use, alcohol use, and exercise.

The AHA/ACC guidelines have many important recommendations, useful tools, and details relevant to primary care clinicians and their consultants. The key preventive points for primary prevention of stroke are summarized below: Every person from birth to death should have access to a primary health care professional, who should screen for and address social determinants of health. Adults with no prior cardiovascular disease and those with high or intermediate risk should adhere to the Mediterranean diet. Screen for sedentary behavior and counsel patients to avoid being sedentary. Recommend that patients engage in regular moderate to vigorous physical activity. Patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk or established cardiovascular disease should receive glucagon-like protein-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists. Patients who require pharmacologic treatment of hypertension should receive at least 2 medications. Clinicians should screen for endometriosis, premature ovarian failure, and early-onset menopause. When hormonal therapy is contemplated, use the lowest estrogenic effect possible. Transgender women who take estrogens should undergo stroke risk factor evaluation and modification.

Aspirin is not recommended for prevention of an initial stroke in low-risk persons. However, the USPSTF recently reviewed primary prevention data for stroke and concluded that aspirin should be encouraged for women between the ages of 55 and 79 years when the potential benefit of a reduction in ischemic strokes outweighs the potential harm of an increase in gastrointestinal hemorrhage. When the 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease is high enough (i.e., >6%-10%), aspirin should be considered.

listitem.strong: Blood pressure, blood sugar, and lipid management

list.listitem: Control blood pressure consistent with national guidelines. Other guidelines suggest at target of <150 mm Hg for patients who are older than 60 (or <140 if there is a history of CVA or TIA) is more desirable. The SPRINT trial found a reduction in a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events including stroke with treatment to a target of 120 mm Hg systolic, but also harms.

The SPRINT trial of patients without diabetes found a reduction in a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events including stroke with treatment to a target of 120 mm Hg systolic, but also harms.

The BPROAD trial found that in older patients with long-term type 2 diabetes and hypertension, decreasing the SBP from 140 mmHg to 120 mmHg will decrease the incidence of CV events 20%. Most of the decrease is due to a reduction in stroke; no other outcomes, including overall risk of death, were statistically lower despite the large number of study participants.
Because of the close balance between benefits and harms, the decision to pursue a lower target should be a shared one.
Treating mild hypertension has been shown to decrease the risk of stroke (NNT for 5 years = 173, although there is a large range in this estimation).
Although tight blood sugar control is advocated, recent studies have found a lack of clinical benefit for a glycohemoglobin level of 6.5% compared with targets of 7.5% to 8.0%.
Advocate healthy lifestyle changes, including smoking cessation, exercise, and weight loss.

Control hyperlipidemia based on national guidelines. A systematic review of 21 studies of primary and secondary prevention found that lipid lowering as primary prevention for stroke is only modestly effective, with a risk reduction of 0.3% over 3 to 6 years (NNT = 333 to prevent one stroke).
AHA/ASA guidelines (2021) recommend that patients with stroke reduce or eliminate alcohol use.
High sensitivity CRP testing has not been shown to predict a vascular-protective response to statin therapy in patients at high risk for stroke.
Stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF)

Warfarin and direct oral anticoagulant therapy is associated with a further reduction in stroke or vascular events over antiplatelet therapy in subjects with nonvalvular AF. Therefore, in patients with AF, a direct oral anticoagulant is recommended by 2021 AHA/ASA guidelines for most patients.

For example, rivaroxaban is similarly as effective as warfarin in preventing stroke in subjects with non-valvular and valvular atrial fibrillation. The oral anticoagulant edoxaban was shown to be of similar efficacy as warfarin in reducing stroke, but may have a lower bleeding risk. Direct oral anticoagulants may be associated with a lower rate of intracranial hemorrhage than warfarin. In a study of patients 80 years and older who were not felt to be candidates for full dose oral anticoagulation, they were randomized to low dose edoxaban (15 mg daily) or placebo. There was a significantly lower risk of stroke or systemic embolism with edoxaban (NNT = 23) although there was also higher risk of GI bleeding (NNTH = 83).

Taking aspirin in addition to warfarin or other oral anticoagulant for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation is associated with increased bleeding with no clear cardiovascular benefit. This combination is not recommended by 2021 AHA/ASA guidelines. For example, in patients with stable CAD and AF, monotherapy with rivaroxaban is preferable to rivaroxaban plus a platelet inhibitor one year after PCI or bypass surgery. Not only were there fewer deaths, there were fewer hemorrhagic strokes and major bleeding events.

Patients with subclinical atrial fibrillation (recurrent episodes lasting between 6 minutes and 24 hours) were randomized to apixaban 5 mg twice daily or aspirin 81 mg once daily. After 3.5 years, there was approximately 1 fewer ischemic stroke and 1 more major bleed for every 250 persons treated with apixaban instead of low-dose aspirin.
In one study, carotid endarterectomy for asymptomatic patients with carotid artery stenosis >60% is associated with a reduced risk of stroke or death (13.4% vs 17.9% with NNT = 25 at 10 years).
For patients with asymptomatic severe carotid stenosis, the annual risk of stroke is 0.9%.
Treating moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea has not been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.
Use of GLP1 receptor agonists in patients with established vascular disease or at very high risk for cardiovascular disease resulted in a 15% relative risk reduction in non-fatal stroke.

Surgical closure of the left atrial appendage during cardiac surgery for another reason safely reduced the risk of ischemic stroke (number needed to treat [NNT] = 43 over 4 years). Since the risk of stroke in the first 30 days after any cardiac surgery is approximately 2%, and the absolute reduction in the risk of stroke with the procedure was only approximately 2%, it wouldn't seem wise to perform this procedure in patients who are not already undergoing cardiac surgery.
Exercise including incidental activity or exercise is strongly associated with reductions in the risk of CV events including stroke.
See "Drug therapy" section for a discussion of the prevention of stroke in patients with known CVD or previous stroke or TIA.
Suspect CVD in patients with a history of transient neurologic symptoms, visual disturbances, fluctuating mental status, seizure, or speech difficulties.C
In patients who are symptomatic, use of CT angiography or combined MRA and carotid duplex ultrasound is accurate and less invasive than digital subtraction angiography.C
Neuroimaging is necessary to determine whether a suspected stroke is ischemic versus hemorrhagic in etiology.

Differential.Differential_Features: Head pain, sensory, and visual disturbances prominent
Symptoms of increased intracranial pressure may be present; may also present with hemorrhage or seizure
Fever, leukocytosis, and hypotension may be apparent
An abrupt loss of consciousness accompanies loss of postural tone with prompt recovery to baseline
Often fluctuating mental status with no focal neurologic deficits
History may reveal evidence of tonic-clonic, repetitive convulsive activity at onset of symptoms
May present with disordered speech but no change in alertness; conversion disorder may present with focal neurologic findings

list.listitem: Suspect CVD in patients with a history of transient neurologic symptoms, visual disturbances, fluctuating mental status, seizure, or speech difficulties.
Auscultation of the carotids to evaluate for carotid stenosis is of limited sensitivity and specificity. An ipsilateral focal bruit is the most sensitive finding for high-grade stenosis.
Options for diagnosing carotid stenosis include Doppler ultrasound, computed tomography angiography (CTA), MRA, and contrast-enhanced MRA.

Digital subtraction angiography is generally considered the gold standard to evaluate carotid stenosis. However, in symptomatic patients suspected of having carotid stenosis, combined MRA and carotid duplex ultrasound are accurate and less invasive.For most patients, ultrasound is an appropriate initial study because of its lower cost, with MRA or digital subtraction angiography reserved for patients who are surgical candidates, or when the ultrasound is equivocal. The combination of MRA and Doppler ultrasound is particularly accurate.

American College of Radiology guidelines recommend Doppler ultrasound, CTA, or MRA as equally appropriate for asymptomatic patients with bruit. For patients with carotid or vertebrobasilar TIA or new focal neurologic deficit, MRI brain, CT head, or MRA head and neck (all with or without contrast) are equally appropriate.
The benefit of carotid endarterectomy for patients with CVD can be predicted using a validated clinical decision rule from the European Carotid Surgery Trialist's Collaborative Group.
The CHAD2DS2-VASc score helps to predict a risk of stroke even in heart failure patient without known atrial fibrillation.
Use evidence-based protocols for the initiation of warfarin and for direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), including in elderly patients.

The risk of stroke in patients with AF can be estimated using validated data from the Framingham study, the SPAF score, or the CHADS2 rule. A clinical rule for predicting 5-year risk of stroke in the elderly also exists.

The risk of stroke immediately following TIA can be estimated using the well-validated ABCD rule. This can help guide the urgency of evaluation, although acute neuroimaging is recommended by recent guidelines for patients with TIA.
In patients with atrial fibrillation, the ABC risk score based on age, cardiac troponin, C-reactive protein, and history of stroke also predicts the risk of stroke.
Data from the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study were used to create a rule for estimating the risk of stroke in patients with diabetes.
If AF is suspected, evaluate the patient for cardioembolic source. If that is normal, evaluate for extracranial disease by carotid ultrasound and MRI/MRA of brain.
If carotid stenosis is greater than 70%, strongly consider referral for carotid endarterectomy.
Endovascular stenting of the carotids is also an option for symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70% or more.
Maximize medical therapy for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. Address smoking, exercise, and obesity.
Prescribe antithrombotics (for most patients: clopidogrel or aspirin plus extended-release dipyridamole).
Blood pressure reduction, regardless of modality, is a cornerstone of management of CVD.A

ACC/AHA guidelines recommend that aspirin and clopidogrel be considered for initiation within 24 hours of high risk TIA (ABCD2 score >= 4) or acute minor stroke (NIHSS <= 3) and continued for up to 21 to 30 days.A

Aspirin, aspirin plus dipyridamole, and clopidogrel are options for the prevention of recurrent stroke; the latter two options are slightly more effective than aspirin alone. The combination of aspirin plus clopidogrel may reduce the risk of ischemic stroke in the short-term, but with a higher bleeding risk.A
Patients with atrial fibrillation and history of stroke should be anticoagulated with a DOA or warfarin; if contraindicated consider an anti-platelet agent.A
Consider carotid endarterectomy or carotid stenting for symptomatic patients with at least 70% carotid stenosis.A

listitem.strong: Patients with recent TIA or minor stroke

list.listitem: ACC/AHA guidelines (2021) recommend that patients with high risk TIA (ABCD2 score >= 4 points) or early minor stroke (NIHSS <= 3 points) should receive dual antiplatelet therapy (e.g. aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 to 30 days. All other patients should receive a single antiplatelet agent, such as low dose aspirin alone.

A network meta-analysis of 9 studies with 22,098 patients comparing DAPT with ticagrelor, DAPT with aspirin, and aspirin alone for patients with minor stroke or TIA found fewer strokes and deaths with either DAPT, but also more hemorrhage with ticagrelor based DAPT than with clopidogrel based DAPT.

A meta-analysis also concluded that DAPT provided generally greater net benefit for patients with minor stroke or TIA, but that the benefit was no greater with treatment longer than 21 to 30 days. This was also supported by a more limited meta-analysis of only 4 studies.

The largest individual trial is the THALES trial that randomized 11,016 with high risk TIA or minor ischemic stroke to ticagrelor + aspirin or aspirin alone. The NNT to prevent one stroke in the next 30 days was 68, and for the composite of fatal or disabling stroke the NNT was 133. Severe bleeding occurred slightly more often with DAPT (NNT = 922).

listitem.strong: Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy: stroke and non-valvular atrial fibrillation

list.listitem: Patients with AF or cardioembolic stroke should be anticoagulated using a direct oral anticoagulant (DOA); aspirin is an alternative, if anticoagulation with a DOA is contraindicated.
If warfarin is chosen, home monitoring of warfarin therapy is not superior to clinic-based testing, but is associated with greater quality of life and satisfaction measures.

Darbigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor that may be slightly more effective than warfarin in preventing stroke among patients with AF, but the benefit may be offset by significantly higher drug costs. In addition, dabigatran therapy may be associated with a slightly higher of acute coronary events. Other novel oral anticoagulants perform similarly to warfarin in reducing stroke from atrial fibrillation.

In an observational cohort study of older patients with atrial fibrillation and a recent stroke, treatment with a DOA was associated with more days alive and not in a hospital or skilled nursing facility, and fewer major adverse cardiovascular events. Patients treated with DOAs also had fewer subsequent deaths and fewer readmissions.

Adding aspirin in addition to oral anticoagulants is not recommended by AHA/ASA 2021 guidelines. It is associated with an increased risk of bleeding without clear benefit. (The exception may be in the setting of mechanical heart valves).
The risks and benefits of novel oral anticoagulants are not necessarily different in patients greater than 75 years old when compared to the general population.

listitem.strong: Anticoagulation and anti-platelet therapy: ischemic (noncardioembolic) stroke

list.listitem: For patients with acute ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation, a meta-analysis concluded that early initiation of DOACs leads to better outcomes, including fewer subsequent strokes and no increase in the risk of intracranial bleeds. For the primary composite outcome of recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), or unclassified stroke at 30 days, the early DOAC group fared better than the later group (2.1% vs 3.0%; p < 0.05, NNT = 111). For individual outcomes, early DOAC initiation decreased the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke (1.7% vs 2.6%; P = .029, NNT = 111) without increasing the risk of symptomatic ICH (0.4% in both arms).

In patients with prior noncardioembolic stroke or TIA, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, clopidogrel, or aspirin with extended-release dipyridamole (APERD) is recommended and can reduce the risk of nonfatal stroke by 28% and fatal stroke by 16%. APERD and clopidogrel are somewhat more effective than aspirin alone, but a decision to use them should include a careful assessment of cost, benefit, and harm. In patients with minor stroke or TIA, adding clopidogrel to aspiring decreases recurrence if started within 24 hours of symptoms.

An individual patient data meta-analysis of 7 trials with 28,982 patients found that clopidogrel was slightly more effective than aspirin for secondary prevention of death, MI or stroke. Using intention-to-treat analysis, the authors report that the overall rate of MACE was lower in the clopidogrel-treated participants (2.6 vs 2.99 per 100 person-years; NNT = 257) and they found no significant difference in the rate of major bleeding (0.71 vs 0.77 per 100 person-years).

Two trials reported a benefit of adding clopidogrel to aspirin to reduce the likelihood of ischemic stroke. However, a meta-analysis does not confirm a benefit to long-term combination therapy, and bleeding risk is significantly increased compared with monotherapy. The most recent AHA/ASA guidelines only recommend clopidogrel + aspirin for patients to prevent recurrent stroke in patients without atrial fibrillation for the first 90 days after stroke.

A large randomized controlled trial (the PROFESS trial) randomized 20,332 patients older than 55 years with recent ischemic stroke to receive APERD or clopidogrel and followed them up for 2.5 years. There was no difference in mortality, myocardial infarction, vascular death, or stroke. Major bleeding complications were more common with APERD, and patients taking APERD had more headaches and were more likely to discontinue the study medication.
Ticagrelor has not been shown to be superior to aspirin in the prevention of recurrent stroke following ischemic stroke or TIA.

For patients presenting with mild-to-moderate acute nonembolic ischemic stroke, treatment with ticagrelor plus aspirin for 30 days resulted in fewer subsequent strokes, but similar overall disability and an increase in severe bleeding, than with aspirin alone (NNT to prevent one stroke or death = 92; NNH to cause one episode of severe bleeding = 263).

For patients with mild-to-moderate acute non-embolic ischemic stroke or TIA and significant ipsilateral atherosclerotic stenosis >30%, treatment with ticagrelor plus aspirin resulted in reduced time to occurence of stroke or death in 30 days, with a NNT of 34.

Anticoagulant therapy offers no additional benefit for patients without NVAF and carries a significant bleeding risk. This appears to be true for patients with a history of TIA and prior stroke of presumed arterial origin. Low-dose aspirin is as effective as high-dose aspirin and minimizes risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.

Extended-release dipyridamole plus low-dose aspirin (Aggrenox) reduces the risk of recurrent stroke by an additional 19% compared with aspirin alone in patients with a previous ischemic stroke. Notably, a mortality benefit for subjects with vascular disease using dipyridamole has not been demonstrated. Similarly, clopidogrel alone is slightly more effective than aspirin in patients with prior stroke, TIA, or with other vascular risk factors.

A meta-analysis of cilostazol (Pletal, an antiplatelet agent that inhibits phosphodiesterase III in platelets and vascular endothelium) versus placebo demonstrated a significant decrease of incidence of cerebrovascular events in the treatment group (RR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.43-0.78) with no increase in bleeding risk. The role of this drug has not been established for patients who are able to take other oral antiplatelet drugs.

Vorapaxar is a platelet PAR-1 receptor blocker that decreases the likelihood of recurrent atherothrombotic events (NNT = 83 over 30 months), but at an increased risk of bleeding (NNTH = 59) and intracerebral hemorrhage (NNTH = 200), especially in patients with prior stroke.
Ticlopidine has been associated with neutropenia and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and is therefore rarely used.

In a randomized trial with 2013 patients, early initiation of a direct oral anticoagulant following ischemic stroke associated with atrial fibrillation was found to be safe and reduced the risk of recurrent stroke. In the early initiation group, DOACs were started within 48 hours of stroke onset for patients with minor or moderate strokes, and on day 6 or 7 after major stroke.

A meta-analysis of 43 studies including 9 RCTs compared different interventions for patients 80 years and older with atrial fibrillation. They found that direct oral anticoagulants were slightly more effective than warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists for prevention of stroke or systemic embolism (NNT19 to 22 versus 23). Edoxaban and apixaban had the most favorable net benefit.

listitem.strong: Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy: cryptogenic embolic stroke

list.listitem: In patients with cryptogenic embolic stroke, an RCT with 5390 patients randomized them to aspirin 100 mg once daily or dabigatran 150 mg twice daily. There was no difference between groups regarding recurrent stroke or major bleeding. There was a small benefit for disabling stroke (0.6% vs 0.9%, NNT = 333/year) but also more clinically relevant non-major bleeds with dabigatran (NNH = 143).

The REDUCE study randomized 560 adults 60 years and older with PFO and a previous cryptogenic stroke 2:1 to antiplatelet therapy + PFO closure or antiplatelet therapy alone. Stroke was less common with closure (NNT = 19, 95% CI 10 to 47).

The ARCADIA study randomized patients with recent cryptogenic stroke and atrial cardiopathy to apixaban twice daily or aspirin 81 mg once daily. There was no difference between groups in rates of recurrent stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, or major hemorrhage.

Lipid-lowering results in a 25% RR reduction in stroke in patients with and without coronary disease. Statins are preferred as the data on other drugs are scant. ACC/AHA guidelines recommend intensive lipid-lowering in patients with previous stroke or TIA with an LDL target of <100 mgdl. A meta-analysis found that statins decrease the risk of stroke in the elderly. While high dose atorvastatin reduces the risk of recurrent stroke, it does not reduce mortality.

A lower LDL target slightly reduced the likelihood of a broad composite outcome (NNT = 43 over 3.5 years), largely by reducing nonfatal strokes (NNT = 77; statistical significance not reported). The benefit was only seen in patients whose index event was a stroke; risk may be increased in those with TIA.

AHA guidelines (2021) recommend an LDL target of <70 mg/dl. A systematic review of secondary prevention studies found that drug therapy for lipid lowering compared with placebo reduced the risk of recurrent stroke (NNT = 87 over 4 years), with a slight increase in hemorrhagic strokes (NNTH = 236) and an increased risk of diabetes.

Statins are effective in preventing major coronary events in patients older than 75 years, but this effect is exclusive to those with established vascular disease (i.e., effective for secondary, not primary, prevention).

Blood pressure reduction to recommended targets, regardless of modality, is a cornerstone to management of CVD. Antihypertensive therapy leads to a 35% to 44% reduction in the incidence of stroke. Some studies have shown an approximately 30% RR reduction in stroke in high-risk patients using angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. Beta-blockers and diuretics have also shown benefit. In general, blood-pressure lowering is the goal and the choice of drug should be tailored to each patient. Other studies challenge the concept that blood pressure lowering is effective after lacunar stroke. In patients with no history of hypertension that have nonetheless suffered a prior stroke or some other form of cardiovascular disease, chronic antihypertensive therapy is associated with reduction in recurrent cardiovascular events (including stroke, with NNT = 185).
Intensive BP treatment reduces the risk of stroke, but has no measured impact on mortality relative to usual care.

In the BPROAD trial of older patients with T2DM, decreasing the SBP from 140 mmHg to 120 mmHg will decrease the incidence of cardiovascular disease–related outcomes slightly. Most of the decrease is due to a reduction in stroke (NNT = 63 over 4 years); no other outcomes, including overall risk of death, were statistically lower despite the large number of study participants. Harms reporting in this study is highly suspect with only 7 episodes of symptomatic hypotension reported in over 6000 older adults treated to a lower target for 4 years. Other studies find rates of 5% to 10%.

In the setting of acute stroke, candesartan for acute blood pressure control did not result in improved mortality and vascular outcomes at 6 months follow-up. Other studies have suggested that tight blood pressure control in acute stroke can be deleterious.
In one randomized controlled trial, using warfarin instead of aspirin for patients with intracranial arterial stenosis and a recent TIA or stroke caused 1 additional death every 2 years.

Treatment with B vitamins or with fish oil has not been shown to reduce future cardiovascular events (including strokes) in patients with a history of ischemic heart disease or stroke. Among patients with diabetic nephropathy, supplements with B vitamins was associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, or overall mortality (NNT to harm = 11 at 32 months). Adhering to a Mediterranean-type diet, however, may be associated with a reduced risk of developing cardiovascular disease.

An RCT of patients with prediabetes and recent stroke (n = 3876) found that those randomized to pioglitazone instead of placebo had a lower rate of stroke, MI, hospitalization, and the subsequent development of diabetes, but at the risk of significant rates of harm, especially fractures, weight gain, and edema.

listitem.strong: "Care Bundles" addressing blood pressure, blood sugar, and other factors

list.listitem: A study in 121 hospitals in 10 mostly low and middle income countries identified patients presenting with acute hemorrhagic stroke. Using a stepped wedge design, a care bundle consisting of intensive blood pressure lowering and rapid management of other physiologic variables resulted in decreased disability at 6 months (OR 0.86; 95% CI 0.76 - 0.97). Additionally, patients in the care bundle group had fewer serious adverse events (16.0% vs 20.1%; p = 0.0098). Secondary outcomes including death at 6 months and hospital discharge by day 7 also favored the care bundle group, but these results were no longer significant in adjusted analyses.
There is insufficient evidence to support routine use of antiepileptic drugs to prevent seizures after stroke.
There is little evidence to direct treating central post stroke pain in an effective manner.
Pioglitazone reduces the likelihood of stroke in patients with a recent stroke or TIA, but has a risk of weight gain, edema, and fracture.
Antidepressants may be helpful for treatment of undesirable emotionalism after stroke.
Antidepressants do not improve motor recovery after stroke.

Symptomatic patients with at least 70% carotid stenosis benefit most from carotid endarterectomy. Surgery for those with symptomatic carotid stenosis of more than 70% reduces the RR of death or disabling stroke by 48% (95% CI, 27%-73%) with an NNT of 15 patients to prevent 1 death or disabling stroke given a 2- to 6-year follow-up.

A study randomized 330 adults age 18 to 65 years with symptomatic unilateral internal carotid or middle cerebral occlusion to medical therapy or medical therapy plus bypass surgery. All patients had experienced a TIA or stroke in the affected region in the past 12 months but now had stable symptoms. There was no difference in any outcomes between groups.
A clinical rule can predict the likelihood of benefit. Patients who require endarterectomy have better outcomes if the procedure is performed within 2 weeks of the most recent event.

Carotid endarterectomy in patients with asymptomatic carotid stenosis reduces the risk of any stroke by 30% over 3 years, but the absolute risk reduction is small. Carotid endarterectomy carries a 3% perioperative stroke or death rate.

Low volume and increasing surgeon age are associated with worse outcomes for carotid endarterectomy. Data regarding technique (i.e., eversion carotid endarterectomy, patch angioplasty versus primary closure, use of shunting, type of anesthesia) are not sufficient to clearly guide therapy.

Antiplatelet agents after endarterectomy appear to reduce risk of stroke. In a study comparing doses of aspirin ranging from 81 to 1300 mg per day following endarterectomy, outcomes were best in those taking 81 or 325 mg daily.

When compared to carotid endarterectomy, carotid artery stenting is associated with a higher periprocedural risk of stroke but lower risk of myocardial infarction. Long-term results (at 2.5 years) show no difference in overall mortality, stroke, or myocardial infarction. Patient and institutional factors may be important in choosing a percutaneous versus surgical approach for subjects with carotid artery stenosis. This has been substantiated by a meta-analysis of 3500 patients in 3 other randomized trials.

A more recent systematic review of 11 studies came to the same conclusion, that stenting carries a higher short-term risk of stroke than carotid artery bypass for patients with asymptomatic carotid stenosis.

A randomized trial in China identified 380 adults with TIA or ischemic stroke that occurred at least 3 weeks previously. They were randomized to stenting + medical therapy or medical therapy alone (DAPT for 90 days, then aspirin, and control of risk factors). There was no difference in outcomes.

Extracranial bypass surgery has not been shown to be more effective at 2-year follow-up than medical therapy alone for the treatment of symptomatic internal carotid artery occlusion. Short-term (30-day) risk of recurrent stroke is reduced with surgical bypass.

In adults with an angiographic diagnosis of unilateral internal carotid artery (ICA) or middle cerebral artery (MCA) occlusion or hemodynamic insufficiency in the MCA territory, a randomized trial with 330 participants found no additional benefit of bypass surgery plus medical therapy over medical therapy alone after 2 years of follow-up in reducing the risk of stroke or death.
Hemicraniectomy increases the likelihood of survival in older subjects with large middle cerebral artery stroke, but neurologic outcomes in these subjects can been poor.
The use of local or general anesthesia during carotid endarterectomy does not affect the incidence of post-procedure stroke or death.

For patients with cryptogenic or recurrent stroke, especially if younger than 55 years, screening for patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defects is sometimes recommended, with repair if a lesion is detected. However, the risk of death is no different for patients with patent foramen ovale provided they are treated with antithrombotics. A recent trial showed that patients with cryptogenic stroke had a reduced risk of recurrence with percutaneous closure of a patent foramen ovale compared to antiplatelet therapy, and a similar rate of recurrence compared to anticoagulation.

The REDUCE study randomized 560 adults 60 years and older with PFO and a previous cryptogenic stroke 2:1 to antiplatelet therapy + PFO closure or antiplatelet therapy alone. Stroke was less common with closure (NNT = 19, 95% CI 10 to 47).

In a systematic review of 5 trials with 1720 patients, the limited evidence suggests that in patients with cryptogenic stroke and PFO, anticoagulant and antiplatelet medications are comparable in effectiveness and risk of major bleeding.
There is insufficient evidence for the effectiveness of memory rehabilitation on functional outcomes, and objective, subjective, and observer-rated memory measures.
The effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation therapy remains unclear.
Smoking cessation and reduction of exposure to environmental cigarette smoke can minimize the risk of thrombotic, embolic, and hemorrhagic stroke.

A population based cluster randomized trial in China compared use of a salt substitute with usual salt consumption. The risk of any stroke was decreased with the salt substitute (NNT = 217 per year) as was fatal stroke (NNT = 500). All-cause mortality was also reduced. Generalizability to western cultures and diets is unclear.

Deep vein thrombosis in the hospitalized patient with acute stroke may be prevented by the use of compression stockings, but evidence is limited. Other guidelines recommend against routine use of compression stockings but note that intermittent compression devices may help in at-risk hospitalized patients where heparin therapy is contraindicated. The use of venous thromboembolus prophylaxis should be individualized based on patient factors rather than routinely started in all stroke patients.
There is inadequate evidence to support the routine use of antiepileptics to prevent seizures after acute stroke.
Bariatric surgery is associated with a reduction in future cardiovascular events, including stroke.
Prophylactic antibiotics are not associated with reducing the risk of pneumonia after stroke in patients with dysphasia.
Training with physical therapy, occupational therapy, and/or speech therapy is associated with reduced disability after stroke.
Chinese herbal medication puerarin has not been shown in clinical trials to improve post-stroke outcomes.
Transcranial magnet stimulation does not appear to improve recovery after stroke; however, studies are ongoing.
Stem cell transplantation has been associated in small trials to reduce neurological impairment, but does not impact overal functional outcomes; safety concerns were not significant.

In a recent meta-analysis, non-pharmacologic therapies for central post stroke pain were evaluated. Some interventions appear effective such as pre-central gyrus stimulation, caloric vestibular stimulation, transcranial direct current stimulation, and bee venom acupuncture point injection. Evidence base for these interventions is weak and require corroboration in further studies.
Active information provision may improve knowledge of stroke care and reduce anxiety and depression, although the magnitude of benefit is unclear.
A systematic review concluded that vestibular rehabilitation therapy is effective for balance (standardized mean difference 0.59, moderate effect) and gait problems post-stroke.

A Cochrane review concluded that evidence for antidepressants to treat emotionalism (e.g. crying, laughing inappropriately or excessively) following stroke is poor. While some studies have found benefit, they were very small and had significant threats to validity.
Evidence for interventions to treat disorders of perception after stroke is lacking.
Approximately 3% of patients with TIA have a stroke within 30 days, 10% within 90 days.B
The risk of stroke immediately following TIA can be estimated using the well-validated ABCD rule.B
The annual rate of nonstroke vascudlar death or myocardial infarction following a stroke is approximately 2%.
Patients with a carotid bruit are at an increased risk of myocardial infarction and cardiovascular death.
Diabetic patients with a carotid bruit are at an increased long-term risk of stroke. A clinical rule can be used to estimate the risk of stroke in patients with diabetes.
The annual rate of nonstroke vascular death or myocardial infarction following a stroke is approximately 2%.
In patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis, prognosis is best in those who have endarterectomy within 2 weeks of most recent cerebrovascular event.

Prognosis has a U-shaped association with blood pressure, with the best outcomes associated with an initial systolic pressure of 150 mm Hg. This does not mean that lowering blood pressure to 150 mm Hg improves outcomes.
An elevated level of troponin T within the first few days after acute stroke is associated with an increased risk of in-hospital death.

The risk of stroke immediately following TIA can be estimated using the well-validated ABCD rule. This can help guide the urgency of evaluation. Overall, approximately 3% of TIA patients have a stroke within 30 days, 10% within 90 days.
The risk of recurrent stroke has been reported to be 1.5% within 2 days, 2.1% within a week, 2.8% within a month, 3.7% within 90 days and 5.1% within a year.
The risk of stroke is similar for persons with post-operative atrial fibrillation versus non-operative AF.
Optimal blood pressure reduction has not been determined, but benefit is associated with average reduction of 10/5 mm Hg.
Patients who smoke should be strongly encouraged to quit.
In patients with previous stroke or TIA, alcohol consumption should be limited to less than three drinks per day for men and one drink per day in nonpregnant women.
Elderly patients are at greatest risk for stroke and are also at the greatest risk for complications from surgical intervention or anticoagulation.
Surgical trials have not included a large number of patients older than 80 years, so cannot detect clear benefit over risk in this subgroup.
Medical therapy trials have included elderly patients and the results support safety and efficacy in this group.
A major adverse cardiovascular event was about twice as likely during 14 years follow-up in children with hypertension compared to those who were normmotensive (6.1% vs 3.1%).
